name: Overhead press

card.summary: A barbell, dumbbell or kettlebell lift pressed from shoulder height to overhead that builds the shoulders, a key part of a broad, V-tapered upper body.
card.aka: shoulder press; strict press; military press; OHP

quick.overview:
The overhead press is a weight-training lift in which the lifter presses a load from the shoulders to overhead, standing or seated. It mainly develops the front of the shoulder (anterior deltoid), and the standing version recruits additional stabilising muscles.[2]

Bigger shoulders widen the upper frame, which lifters use to build a V-shaped physique. T Nation members debate whether it is needed for hypertrophy when bench work and lateral raises already train the deltoids.[3]
quick.how: Lifters use barbells, dumbbells or kettlebells, seated or standing, with variations such as the push press (leg dip for momentum) and one-arm or alternating presses. It is programmed as part of upper-body or push sessions.
quick.risks: As with any heavy lifting, form and load management matter; shoulder and low-back discomfort are common topics in training forums. No specific safety section is given in encyclopedic sources.

lead: The overhead press, also called the shoulder press, strict press or military press, is an upper-body lift in which a barbell, dumbbells or kettlebells are pressed from shoulder level to overhead, seated or standing.[2]

It is primarily used to develop the anterior deltoid, and standing variants add balance and stabiliser demand.[2] For appearance, lifters use it to build shoulder size and width, which supports a broader-looking upper body.
It was once part of the clean and press in Olympic weightlifting until 1972, and bodybuilders have long used strict presses to isolate the deltoids; strongmen also use logs and axles.[2]

chain: Progressive loading of the deltoids and triceps
Larger shoulders, wider frame and V-taper
angle.text: Training the overhead press drives growth in the shoulders, which lifters use to widen the upper body. Some experienced lifters argue lateral raises and bench variations cover shoulder hypertrophy without it.

infobox: Shoulder press, military press, strict press

paras: The lift is done holding a weight at shoulder height and pressing overhead; standing versions demand more balance and engage more muscles. Variations include the push press, unilateral and alternating presses.[2]
The standing press was part of the clean and press in Olympic weightlifting until it was removed in 1972, because judges found technique hard to evaluate. It remains a strongman staple.[2]

A 2026 T Nation thread asks whether the overhead press is redundant for hypertrophy if someone already does flat and incline bench presses and lateral raises, arguing the front delts get ample work from bench and that dropping it improves recovery.[3]

No studies found specific to the overhead press and appearance. Related studies cover resistance training generally, for example velocity-based versus percentage-based loading on strength and power.[4]

timeline.event: Clean and press removed from Olympic weightlifting.[2]

lore.intro: Lifters debate the overhead press's place in physique training.[3]

claims.claim: The overhead press is redundant for shoulder size if you bench and do lateral raises
claims.believers: A T Nation poster argues the anterior delts are well trained by flat and incline benching and medial delts by lateral raises, so removing the press frees recovery for shrugs or rear-delt work.[3]
claims.experts: No published study has tested this program question directly.
